claims.text: Finite-temperature DFT combined with anharmonic phonon calculations adjusted for atomic-scale disorder can explicitly decouple lattice and electronic thermal transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
The new approach will predict lattice thermal conductivity with at least 30% less error than conventional Debye-temperature-based methods.
The modeled HfNbTaTiZr is a defect-free but compositionally disordered bulk crystal.
The computational scheme separately models lattice vibrations and electronic contributions.
The lattice model includes anharmonic phonon scattering.
The applicable temperature range is 200–1200 K.
The applicable samples must contain less than 1 wt.% oxygen.
A 200–1200 K range and oxygen content below 1 wt.% match the controlled conditions of prior experiments and simulations.
Multiple principal elements create atomic-scale disorder in HfNbTaTiZr.
Atomic-scale disorder creates a complex landscape for phonon scattering and electron-phonon coupling.
Explicit treatment of temperature-dependent anharmonicity and electron-phonon interactions overcomes oversimplifications in Debye-based and defect-free simulation methods.
Treating anharmonicity and electron-phonon interactions improves separation of lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions.
The model will reduce lattice-conductivity root-mean-square prediction error by at least 30% relative to earlier methods.
Prior approaches estimated total thermal conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m) at high temperatures.
Prior approaches either conflated lattice and electronic transport or relied on Debye-temperature approximations that do not capture HfNbTaTiZr's atomistic complexity.
The approach is reliable only above 200 K because lattice and electronic transport are sufficiently decoupled there.
Enhanced impurity scattering, including that associated with higher oxygen contamination, limits applicability.
Time-domain thermoreflectance can provide lattice thermal conductivity decoupled from the electronic contribution in these samples.
Failure to obtain at least 30% lower prediction error than conventional models would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure of the predicted lattice conductivity to agree with isolated lattice-conductivity measurements within experimental error across 200–1200 K would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The conditions include 200 K, while the boundary says the approach is reliable only above 200 K.
